t: Count the Number of Good Partitions — Cut Points via Last Occurrence
o: A partition into contiguous subarrays is good iff equal values stay together. Between index i and i+1 a cut is allowed exactly when nums[i]'s last occurrence is at most i — otherwise cutting would separate copies of the same value. Every subset of allowed cuts yields exactly one good partition, so the answer is 2^(number of allowed cuts). Example [1,2,3,4] has 3 allowed cuts → 8; [1,2,1,3] has 1 → 2.
k: Cut after i is legal iff last[nums[i]] == i (for i < n-1).
Independent cuts combine multiplicatively: answer = 2^cuts mod 1e9+7.

a.i: Record the last index of each value, sweep left to right maintaining the furthest last-occurrence seen so far; whenever that equals the current index (and i < n-1), a cut is allowed.
s: Build last[v] = final index of v.
Sweep i from 0 to n-2, keeping far = max(last[nums[0..i]]).
Count i where far == i; return pow(2, count, MOD).
a.t: O(n) — one pass to record last occurrences, one sweep to count cuts
a.sp: O(n) — hash map of last occurrences

w: This is identical in spirit to the 'partition labels' / 'merge intervals' family. Only one meaningful approach exists; a DP over intervals would be strictly heavier. Pitfalls: excluding the cut after the final index (it is not a real cut), and forgetting the modulus on the power. Follow-up: count partitions where each block must satisfy an additional property (e.g., sum divisible by k) — then it becomes a prefix-sum DP.
